How KEA works

KEA is a signer you control. It watches for transactions, checks each one against rules you published, and signs only the ones that match. It never builds a transaction, never holds anyone else's money, and never takes instructions from the thing asking it to sign.

The one idea

Most systems that move money for you need to be trusted with the power to move money. KEA splits that in two: whoever assembles a transaction holds no key that can approve it, and whoever holds a key approves only what matches something published in advance.

There are five jobs here, and the useful part is that they can be five different parties — whoever wrote the rule need not be the one proposing, and neither need be the one holding a key:

JobWho does itWhat they hold
Write the ruleanyone — a business, a person, a scriptNothing at runtime. They write down what they are willing to pay, and on what conditions, and publish it.
Aska bot, a page, a personNo key that can approve anything. It proposes; that is all.
Assemble and holdthe pool (kpool)No keys at all. It builds the transaction, holds it, and relays it exactly as it was signed — it adds no signature of its own, because it has none to add.
ApproveKEA — one or more devicesA key. The only thing it will use it for is adding one approval to a transaction matching a published rule.
SettleHederaThe ledger. It alone decides whether the signatures gathered are sufficient, and either settles or refuses.
The sentence worth remembering

You publish what you are willing to do; someone proposes it; a venue assembles it; and a signer you control approves it only if it matches what you published. Nobody in the middle can move your funds, because nobody in the middle has your key.

One approval, not a release

A signer adds a signature. It does not decide the outcome and it does not release anything. If the account requires two of three devices, one signature moves nothing at all — the transaction simply sits there a little less unsigned than before. The ledger, and only the ledger, decides when what has been gathered is enough.

This distinction matters more than it sounds: it is why adding a signer is safe, why a signer going quiet cannot strand your funds, and why no single device on the list is a single point of failure unless you built it that way.

How the pieces connect

KEA talks outbound only. It opens a connection to the pool and to a public Hedera mirror node; nothing connects to it. That is what lets a signer live on a phone behind a home router with no ports open and no fixed address.

The machine: what happens to one transaction

This is the part worth understanding properly. Think of a transaction as a ball dropped into the top of a machine. It falls through a series of gates. Every gate can drop it out, and every drop-out has a name. Only a ball that clears every gate reaches the bottom and gets signed.

What each gate is actually doing

GateThe questionWhy it matters
policyWhat is the identity of these rules?The rule document is hashed, and that hash is its id. The id is computed, never read from what arrived — so nobody can relabel one deal as another.
authorityIs this id on my list?The allowlist belongs to the signer, not the request. This is the line that makes an untrusted venue safe: it can ask for anything, and get a refusal.
inputsWere only the declared inputs supplied?A rule declares what it accepts. Anything extra is refused rather than ignored.
decodeWhat do these bytes actually move?Read from the raw transaction, never from the friendly summary next to it. The summary is a claim; the bytes are the thing that will execute.
observeWhat does the chain say right now?The signer re-fetches every fact itself from a public mirror node. Nothing the raiser supplied is taken on trust.
derive / requireDo the conditions hold?The rule's own conditions — a deadline, a balance, a winner, an owner — evaluated against what was just observed.
reproduceIf I built this myself, would I get the same thing?The strongest check. The signer constructs the transaction from the rules and compares it leg by leg with what it was handed. Any difference is a refusal, not a warning.
capsIs this more than I agreed to approve in an hour?A ceiling per asset, counting what this signer has already signed. The backstop for a rule that turns out to be wrong.
signersDoes this even need my key?Derived from the bytes: which of my accounts are debited, or pay the fee. If none, there is nothing to do.
This is already machine-readable

Every gate emits { id, status, detail } as the transaction passes — pass, fail, refuse, skip or error. That list comes back on every decision, including refusals. So a picture of the ball falling through the machine is not a thing that needs building from scratch; the data is already there, waiting to be drawn.

Two rules that never bend

A refusal is loud. Every refusal names the gate that stopped it. A signer that silently does nothing is indistinguishable from a broken one, which is the failure the dashboard exists to end.

A hint is never authority. Anything that narrows what a signer looks at — a filter, a notification — is an optimisation only. The signer re-checks everything after reading it, so a wrong hint costs a missed transaction, never a wrong signature.

How signatures add up

KEA does not know or care whether its signature is enough. It holds a key, it signs, and it posts the signature back to the pool. Whether that is sufficient is the ledger's question.

A Hedera account can require one key, or several, or a nested arrangement — "any one of these three", or "any two of these three", or "this one, or any two of those three". So a payout can be made to need two separate devices held by two separate people, neither able to act alone. Nothing in the signer changes to do that; you change the account's key.

Why that is the interesting part

The approval rule lives outside the venue and outside any custodian. "Sign only transactions matching these published rules, under these limits, and only when two of these three devices agree" is an authorisation policy that no single compromised machine can override.

Ways to run a signer

A signer is its own thing, running beside your application — not inside it. It watches the pool, and it happens to hold a key your application's accounts depend on. That separation is the point: your application can be rewritten, redeployed or compromised without the key moving.

ShapeGood forStatus
Node.js process
a server, a Raspberry Pi, a phone in Termux		Unattended signing. The usual choice for a service that must keep running.Working today.
Browser / PWAA person approving on screen, or a device that should only sign when somebody opens it. Installable, no install ceremony.Working today as a web app; the same decision code as the Node body.
Native appA phone as a dedicated signing device, with the key held by the platform's own secure storage.Planned.
Edge / small nodesSeveral cheap signers in different places, so no single location holds enough keys to reach a threshold on its own.Follows naturally — a signer is outbound-only and needs no inbound address.

All of these run the same decision. The checks in the machine above are one piece of code with no keys and no network of its own; each shape only supplies the surroundings — how it hears about a transaction, where the key is kept, how it reads the chain. That is why a phone and a server reach identical verdicts, and why adding a new shape does not mean rewriting the rules.

Running more than one

Signers do not coordinate and do not need to. Each hears about the same transaction, decides independently, and posts its own signature. Two signers reaching the same conclusion is not duplication — it is the point. If they disagree, the disagreement is visible rather than silent: that is exactly what the dashboard is for.

Using KEA yourself

Work in progress

KEA currently lives inside a larger backend repository and is being separated into its own public repository. The shape below is what integrating will look like; the repository link and the package name will be filled in here when the split lands. Nothing described above is speculative — it is all running — but the packaging is not finished.

What you will need

  1. Rules you have published. One document per thing you are willing to pay for, listed in a catalogue, each identified by its own hash.
  2. An account whose key you control, set to require whichever devices you want — one, or two of three, or whatever suits what is at stake.
  3. A key on each device, generated on that device. The public half goes onto the account; the private half never leaves.
  4. A config file per signer: which network, where the pool is, which catalogue and which exact hash of it, the caps, and a reference to the key — never the key itself.

The shape of it

{
  "network": "testnet",
  "pool":    { "base": "https://<the pool>" },
  "mirror":  "https://testnet.mirrornode.hedera.com/api/v1",

  "keys":    { "0.0.YOURACCOUNT": "env:MY_SIGNING_KEY" },

  "deals": [
    { "from": "catalogue",
      "dir":  "vendor/<your app>/deals",
      "pin":  "sha256:<the exact catalogue you reviewed>",
      "caps": { "<asset>": 1000000 } }
  ],

  "presence": { "level": "advertise", "everyMs": 30000 }
}

Three things in that file carry most of the safety:

  • pin — the signer refuses to start if the catalogue on disk does not hash to this. Updating your rules is a deliberate act: review, then change one line.
  • caps — the most this signer will approve per asset per hour, whatever the rules say.
  • keys — a reference (env:NAME or a file path), so the config can be committed, reviewed and shared without ever containing a secret.

Bringing one up

  1. Check before you run. A doctor command answers the questions in the order they bite: is the config valid, is the key present, does the chain accept it, can this device reach the pool — and, importantly, whether this key is enough on its own or only counts towards a group.
  2. Watch first. Start in dry run. It decides on everything and signs nothing, so you can read its verdicts against real traffic before it has any power.
  3. Then let it sign. One flag.
  4. Rehearse the failure. Stop the signers that can act alone, and confirm the remaining ones do what you expect. Do this before it matters, not after.
Announcing is optional, and off by default

A signer can announce itself so it appears on the dashboard — its name, whether it will actually sign, what it is watching. That is opt-in: a signer says nothing unless its config or its command line turns it on. Nothing announced is secret, but the correlation — these keys, this device, awake at this minute — is new information, so it is a choice rather than a default. Announcing never affects whether anything gets signed; a quiet signer signs exactly as much as a talkative one.

Words used here

WordMeans
dealA published document saying what you are willing to pay, to whom, and under what conditions. Its hash is its name.
catalogueThe list of deals an application publishes. It has its own hash, so "the rules as of now" is a single value you can pin.
pool / kpoolWhere transactions wait for signatures. It assembles and holds; it never holds keys, and it forgets after about an hour.
raiserWhoever asked for the transaction to be built. Holds no key that can approve it.
mirror nodeA public read-only view of Hedera. How a signer checks facts for itself.
presenceA signer announcing that it is here, signed with a key it claims to hold — so the claim is evidence, not a note somebody wrote.
dry runDecide everything, sign nothing.
capThe most a signer will approve per asset per hour, regardless of what the rules permit.

Written 2026-09-17 alongside the signers dashboard. The gates described here are the ones the signer actually runs, in this order, and each one's name matches what appears in a decision's own check list.
